subject: puzzling facet_grid, data, and group interaction

messages.author: 9e1d805a26f6d719
messages.subject: puzzling facet_grid, data, and group interaction
parts:
Hi, I'm trying to annotate a facet_grid plot, and can't get everything to work at once. I've reproduced the problem with the mtcars dataset:


a <- data.frame(x=10,xend=10,y=1,yend=3)

# this works:
qplot(mpg, wt, data=mtcars, group=carb, geom="line") + facet_grid(cyl ~ vs)

# and this works:
qplot(mpg, wt, data=mtcars, geom="line") + facet_grid(cyl ~ vs) + geom_segment(data=a, aes(x=x,y=y,xend=xend,yend=yend), size=2, color="grey")

# and this even works:
qplot(mpg, wt, data=mtcars, color=carb, geom="line") + facet_grid(cyl ~ vs) + geom_segment(data=a, aes(x=x,y=y,xend=xend,yend=yend), size=2, color="grey")

# but this doesn't:
qplot(mpg, wt, data=mtcars, group=carb, geom="line") + facet_grid(cyl ~ vs) + geom_segment(data=a, aes(x=x,y=y,xend=xend,yend=yend), size=2, color="grey")

Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object "carb" not found


I can't figure this out. There are some (for lack of a better term) variable scoping issues with ggplot, or maybe with the underlying packages, that completely baffle me. Could someone explain why the geom_segment object affects whether or not the group works? (And, of course, how to work around this problem?)

Thanks Hadley et al!

 -Harlan

> Hi, I'm trying to annotate a facet_grid plot, and can't get everything to
> work at once. I've reproduced the problem with the mtcars dataset:

>
> a <- data.frame(x=10,xend=10,y=1,yend=3)
>
> # this works:
> qplot(mpg, wt, data=mtcars, group=carb, geom="line") + facet_grid(cyl ~ vs)
>
> # and this works:

> geom_segment(data=a, aes(x=x,y=y,xend=xend,yend=yend), size=2, color="grey")
>
> # and this even works:
> qplot(mpg, wt, data=mtcars, color=carb, geom="line") + facet_grid(cyl ~ vs)
> + geom_segment(data=a, aes(x=x,y=y,xend=xend,yend=yend), size=2,
> color="grey")
Because the grey colour overrides the colour mapping.

> # but this doesn't:
> qplot(mpg, wt, data=mtcars, group=carb, geom="line") + facet_grid(cyl ~ vs)
> + geom_segment(data=a, aes(x=x,y=y,xend=xend,yend=yend), size=2,
> color="grey")

Try geom_segment(data=a, aes(x=x,y=y,xend=xend,yend=yend, group =
NULL), size=2, color="grey")

Or spell it out explicitly with ggplot:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(mpg, wt)) +
geom_line(aes(group = carb) +
geom_segment(data=a, aes(x,y,xend=xend,yend=yend), size=2, color="grey") +
facet_grid(cyl ~ vs)

Or spell it out explicitly with ggplot:

 geom_line(aes(group = carb) +
 geom_segment(data=a, aes(x,y,xend=xend,yend=yend), size=2, color="grey") +
 facet_grid(cyl ~ vs)

Well, that works (and the corresponding change on my actual plot works too), but I have absolutely no intuition why. Why doesn't the data=a in the geom_segment call over-ride the surrounding grouping? You can't assume that changing the scope (by the new data) will give the same variables, can you? The fact that plots, which have an inherently hierarchical structure, are squished into a linear sequence in the ggplot2 syntax, just hurts my head. Sometimes later layers affect earlier ones, and sometimes they don't.

Much as I like some aspects of ggplot2, if I continue to have to email the list for many of the plots I make, I'm going to have to abandon it, sad to say. So far, it's been much faster to tediously export my data, import it into xmgrace, and manually set all of the little details that ggplot2 does so nicely. Hopefully the ongoing and very rapid improvements in the package and the documentation will help me through this.

 -Harlan

In your example this is a pain, but most of the time this is really
helpful - you just make sure your variable names match and you don't
need to worry about redefining all the aesthetic mappings. Think
about the ggplot call as setting the defaults that all of the other
layers inherit - you can make the defaults as comprehensive, or not,
as you like.

> The fact that plots, which have an inherently hierarchical structure, are
> squished into a linear sequence in the ggplot2 syntax, just hurts my head.
> Sometimes later layers affect earlier ones, and sometimes they don't.

Layers _never_ affect other layers. Scales, coords and facetting all
override previous specifications.

> Much as I like some aspects of ggplot2, if I continue to have to email the
> list for many of the plots I make, I'm going to have to abandon it, sad to
> say. So far, it's been much faster to tediously export my data, import it
> into xmgrace, and manually set all of the little details that ggplot2 does
> so nicely. Hopefully the ongoing and very rapid improvements in the package
> and the documentation will help me through this.

You might want to switch to using ggplot() instead of qplot() -
sometimes it helps to be more explicit about what's going on.

Hadley

messages.author: fc22cb727156ff4f
messages.subject: Re: puzzling facet_grid, data, and group interaction
parts: On 2009-May-15  , at 15:42 , Harlan Harris wrote:

> You might want to switch to using ggplot() instead of qplot() -
> sometimes it helps to be more explicit about what's going on.
>
> Yes, I'll do that.

From the point of view of someone who learned ggplot, I would also
strongly advise to use the ggplot construct as much and as soon as
possible. qplot is nice to lure users into using ggplot, because the
syntax is close enough to that of other plotting systems. However, the
true nature and power of ggplot only became apparent once I used
ggplot().

I would even advise to use ggplot() as an empty container and build
the plot layer by layer, specifying almost everything in each geom. It
is more explicit what the variables in each layer are if you do
something like

ggplot() + geom_point(data=foo, mapping=aes(x=x, y=y)) +
geom_path(data=bar, aes(x=x, y=y, colour=value))

Later down the road, you can recompress is in the form

ggplot(aes(x=x,y=y)) + geom_point(data=foo) + geom_path(data=bar,
aes(colour=value))

where the aesthetics are shared by all later geoms. But I find that
most of the time there is little difference. Indeed, when I have two
sets of data with exactly the same names, it's usually that they are
on the exact same scale (same coordinates) so I can easily merge the
dataframes (with merge()) and use that in ggplot. Otherwise, the two
data frames are separated enough that each needs a complete geom
specifications anyway.

To sum, up, I would advise you to
- use constructs like
ggplot(foo, aes(x=x,y=y, colour=bar)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth()
when you have one simple data frame as input
- switch to full specification
ggplot() + geom_point(data=foo, aes(x=x,y=y, colour=bar)) +
geom_path(data=bar, aes(x=lon, y=lat, size=value))
as soon as your data source gets a little more complex.

I hope that helps and that you'll keep using ggplot.

JiHO
---
http://jo.irisson.free.fr/

parts:
JiHO, this is some really good advice, and thank you for taking the time to write it.
As with any complicated system, it's difficult for the authors of that system to fully understand what novices (such as myself) find difficult about that system. I'm trying to learn several things at once -- the "words" of ggplot2 (geom_line, scale_x_continuous, etc.) and the "grammar" of ggplot2. But the grammar has two properties that make it difficult to learn. First, it doesn't quite fit into the conceptual structures that I'm used to. It has the syntax (the +s and ()s) of a programming language, but if you think about it that way, the scoping rules make no sense whatsoever, with weird backwards dependencies and a total disregard for locality. It's internally defining a hierarchical representation of a plot, like what one might think of in a more traditional drawing or plotting system, but in a very sparse way, and there's currently no good way of seeing that representation to check whether the translation from the linear language to the hierarchical language is working. And second, there are a large number of ways of doing everything, so you can't easily "chunk" useful phrases and use them elsewhere (as adults do when learning a new spoken language). It's as if you were learning a new language, but half the people used a variant like Latin, where you can put anything in any order as long as you case-mark everything, and some people used a variant like Chinese, where there is a standard order for everything, and some people used a variant like Japanese, where everything is backward and written in three different alphabets. ggplot2's extremely flexible syntax may make it difficult to be widely adopted by the R community, without significant pedagogical changes. In particular, it may be possible to teach ggplot2 by defining a rigid subset of the syntax that allows you to do everything, but also allows people to apply their existing conceptual knowledge of how programming languages work. Combined with a better tool for visualizing the resulting hierarchical plot structure, ggplot2's remarkable elegance and power may become more accessible. I would urge Hadley and others working on "grammar for graphics" ideas to spend some time thinking about the incomplete cognitive representations that learners of the systems are using, and how those misconceptions can cause ongoing problems with learning. Perhaps the next major upgrade to the system could involve some thoughts along these lines.

I appreciate y'all's indulgence in my little rant... I really want to use ggplot2, but am frustrated by my own inability to fully figure it out.

 -Harlan

messages.author: b26ea422f70d3a1f
messages.subject: Re: puzzling facet_grid, data, and group interaction
parts:
Harlan,

If I may counter-rant: It doesn't matter if ggplot2 fits into any
conceptual structure that you're used to. If you want a tool that
does, use base graphics or lattice. It should definitely NOT change to
match your pre-existing concepts of how graphs work or what graphs
are. It has a different philosophy on purpose, and I think your main
problem comes from trying to force it into your programming-language
framework -- which does not really work -- and it causes a cascade of
misunderstanding.

My first question for you would be: why exactly are you using ggplot2?
Because it's easy to make a particular kind of graph with it? Because
the defaults look nicer to you? To be blunt, those are not reasons to
use ggplot2. I've recreated certain ggplot2 graphs in lattice, for
various reasons. Anything you can do in ggplot2, you can do it in
lattice, though not with the same philosophy. What ggplot2 offers is a
different philosophy, and that's what you seem to be objecting to.

Now don't get me wrong. I've had a similar conversation about 5 months
ago when I first picked up ggplot2. But more on that later... First,
some more questions. (Not being facetious or rhetorical here, I
actually would like to see answers.)

You keep mentioning that ggplot2 is hierarchical. In what way? Please
give some examples. I see it as refreshingly orthogonal, and that's a
huge boost over alternatives that blur concepts together. I really
can't think of anything that's hierarchical about ggplot2.

(I'll say I had problems when I first came to ggplot2 because of how
some of the orthogonal concepts are described and broken out. They
make sense overall, but as one example, "scale" means something very
different in ggplot2 than what you might think of coming from another
background. I've tried to think of perhaps a better way of describing
the concept than "scale", and offered various suggestions to Hadley of
how the documentation might step you through the concepts in finer
increments, to help dispel misunderstandings early. But think as I
may, it's hard to come up with a correct way to describe "scale" that
is accurate and yet avoids the misunderstandings that I had with
"scale".)

You keep mentioning its "programming language syntax" with "+'s and
()'s", but it has no syntax of its own, only the R's syntax, which ALL
alternatives must cope with. Parentheses are used for function calls,
as in every other package you will ever use in R. How is ggplot2
somehow different than anything else you do in R, parentheses-wise?

(Yes, it uses "+" where other graphics packages do not, but that is
because you can explicitly add to a graph object, which alternatives
really cannot do. (Base graphics, for example, has a half-baked system
where you are essentially drawing nearly-unrelated graphs to a window
without erasing between draws. This will paint you into a corner oft-
times, or cause you to jump through hoops to avoid issues that a
computer should handle for you.) It's certainly not that odd in light
of other kinds of data structures that can be combined in many
languages with "+", including things like "Hello" + " there!".)

You mention "locality" as if this were a programming language with
scope. What do you see the locality that it should be honoring and how
does it break down?

Having several ways to do something is a benefit, not a drawback. R
certainly provides several ways to approach any one task syntactically
-- if only something as basic as implicit versus explicit iteration --
and if you want to find the "right" or "best" package to accomplish a
particular task it gets crazy-confusing. Your analogy with different
human languages doesn't really do much for me. Are you objecting to
flexibility in general, or in the how Hadley's documentation teaches
ggplot2, or where?

In addition to my initial problems with concepts like "scale" (above),
there is a complication that I cannot put my finger on. I think there
are two issues arising from ggplot2 being very Lego-like: you have
many, many pieces that you can plug together. Which leads to:

1. It causes many subtle bugs to creep in. Which can result in
something you think SHOULD work not working and you get frustrated
with stupid ggplot2. It feels like ggplot2's just being opaque and non-
intuitive, but in fact it's a bug and what you're doing actually
should be working but it just feels like it's being weird and you're
left asking, "What's the 'ggplot2 way' of doing things that I'm not
getting?"

2. You can do some incredibly sophisticated graphs with just a few
characters in ggplot2, which can let you get deep into the woods
without realizing that you don't actually understand some basic
concepts. The alternative, however, is not very palatable: make it
work like other packages, where you have to do a lot of coding to get
what you want, so you have to understand everything along the way or
it simply doesn't happen.

3. The error messages are not always the best. I think Hadley's
admitted to that and is looking into what he can do about that.
(Unfortunately, it could be a pretty deep-seated problem that doesn't
admit to a good solution without a rewrite.)

The bottom line, for me, is that it seems that you're trying to push
ggplot2 into your pre-existing frameworks and "programming language"
is the closest framework for you and from that viewpoint, ggplot2
won't make much sense. But specific examples would help everyone
understand what your pointing out.

Wayne

On Sat, May 16, 2009 at 10:29 PM, Wayne Folta <wd...@mac.com> wrote:
If I may counter-rant: It doesn't matter if ggplot2 fits into any
conceptual structure that you're used to. If you want a tool that
does, use base graphics or lattice. It should definitely NOT change to
match your pre-existing concepts of how graphs work or what graphs
are.

Speaking for myself (though I suspect that Harlan would agree), I very much like ggplot's conceptual structure of graphs.  It makes much more sense to me than base graphics or lattice graphics.  That is not the issue at all.

What I have had more trouble with is the notation for that conceptual structure.  I find it hard to put my finger on what exactly the problem is, but the use of '+' (normally a commutative, associative operator) to express a rather complicated hierarchical relationship might be part of it. Another part of it is the handy (but again complicated) defaults.

I find Mike Lawrence's suggestion to use only 'layer' intriguing and might try it.  Maybe that will make things simpler for me. Having three different notations defined for ggplot (qplot, geom_xxx, and layer) is confusing.  I guess Hadley assumed that readers of his book will be coming from R base graphics, but if I were teaching R + plotting, I would want to skip base graphics entirely....

It has a different philosophy on purpose, and I think your main problem comes from trying to force it into your programming-language framework -- which does not really work -- and it causes a cascade of misunderstanding.

Not sure what you mean here.  ggplot *is* a programming language, and it is also embedded into a programming language.  To the extent that ggplot's semantics are inconsistent with those of the embedding language, there is bound to be confusion.

...You keep mentioning that ggplot2 is hierarchical. In what way? Please
give some examples.

I don't know if this is what Harlan had in mind, but for me, the very simplest example is things like:

    ggplot(data=qq) +
        geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) +
        geom_point(aes(x=c,y=d)) +
        coordxxx()

which really means something like

     with( list(data=qq),
               coordxxx(     # coord applies to the whole stack of layers
                  stack_layers( geom_point( aes(x=a,y=b) ),   # a and b are w.r.t. qq
                                         geom_point(aes(x=c,y=d)) ) ) )
 
(note the nesting)

By the way, a strange (but not necessarily very practical) case I constructed:

     test <- data.frame(a=1:4,b=4:1)
     ggplot() + local({
             qq <- test
             geom_point(data=qq,aes(x=a,y=b) )
            } ) # works fine

     test <- data.frame(x=1:4,y=4:1)
     ggplot() + local({
             qq <- test
             k <- 3
             geom_point(data=qq,aes(x=x,y=y^k) )
            } )
# error: object "k" not found


1. ...something you think SHOULD work not working and you get frustrated

with stupid ggplot2. It feels like ggplot2's just being opaque and non-
intuitive, but in fact it's a bug and what you're doing actually
should be working but it just feels like it's being weird and you're
left asking, "What's the 'ggplot2 way' of doing things that I'm not
getting?"
Yes, I have run into this too.

3. The error messages are not always the best. I think Hadley's
admitted to that and is looking into what he can do about that.

Yes, I have raised this issue, too.
 
               -s

> qq <- test
> k <- 3
> geom_point(data=qq,aes(x=x,y=y^k) )
> } )
> # error: object "k" not found

Since k is used in the aes call, it needs to be in the data for ggplot
to find it; i.e.

k=3
geom_point(data=qq,aes(x=x,y=y^k)) # not OK

qq$k=3
geom_point(data=qq,aes(x=x,y=y^k)) # OK

geom_point(data=qq,aes(x=x,y=y^3)) # OK

JiHO

messages.subject: Re: puzzling facet_grid, data, and group interaction
parts: On 2009-May-16  , at 22:29 , Wayne Folta wrote:

> The bottom line, for me, is that it seems that you're trying to push
> ggplot2 into your pre-existing frameworks and "programming language"
> is the closest framework for you and from that viewpoint, ggplot2
> won't make much sense.

I would like to second that. My impression after reading your first
question and "rant" is that your problem comes from knowing too much
already. Your preconceived ideas are impairing your learning of
ggplot. To re-use your metaphor: have you ever noticed how hard it is
to learn a new language for grown-ups, while kids/teenagers pick that
in a blast?. So, even though this is just commonplace talk, I think
you should try to forget a bit what you know and come to ggplot with a
fresher mind.

Not having much experience in base R graphics or extended knowledge or
programming languages structure, I found ggplot very intuitive: you're
just building the plot layer by layer, linking the properties of your
data to graphical representations. Sure there are some edge cases and
some less intuitive stuff (the scales in particular can be tricky).
But overall, the fact that ggplot rests upon a real "system" (the
grammar or graphics) makes it clearer than other plotting systems.

Finally, regarding the implementation, I agree that having several
ways of doing the same thing is confusing. I tend to prefer simple,
reliable "things" over fancy, hyper-configurable ones. As other
posters, I think that having ggplot() + layer() + scale() would have
been sufficient, even though the syntax is longer (but I started with
ggplot + geom so now I stick to that). However, I also understand the
necessity of providing qplot or other simplified, more usual,
interfaces.
The thing is, each of us does not *have* to use all the complexity.
You can choose to use only a subset of the language and stick to it,
to ease up the learning. I recommended ggplot() + geom_* earlier.
That's probably the most documented. But if you want a very strong and
conservative structure, ggplot + layer is probably better.

JiHO

parts: Stavros,

> I don't know if this is what Harlan had in mind, but for me, the
> very simplest example is things like:
>
> ggplot(data=qq) +
> geom_point(aes(x=a,y=b)) +
> geom_point(aes(x=c,y=d)) +
> coordxxx()
>
> which really means something like
>
> with( list(data=qq),
> coordxxx( # coord applies to the whole stack of
> layers
> stack_layers( geom_point( aes(x=a,y=b) ), # a
> and b are w.r.t. qq
>
> geom_point(aes(x=c,y=d)) ) ) )
>

Good example!

I've rewritten this reply multiple times, and finally think I see the
core issue here: your "really means" rephrasing of the ggplot2 code is
execution-oriented. It is the way that ggplot2 would work if it had
the same philosophy as base graphics: when geom_point() is called, it
would literally draw stuff on the page.

But rather, ggplot2 is about creating an object and setting
properties, then causing it to plot by printing it. It's object-
oriented, and the ggplot(data=qq) is creating an object with several
default properties and one explicit property. The coordxxx() is
setting some more properties of this object. The geom_point()'s are
setting properties, which themselves are objects which inherit some
properties from the ggplot2 object and have some properties of their
own.

So there is a hierarchy, but it's an OO kind of hierarchy. It takes
the human phrasing of a graph: "Create a graph using data from the
dataframe qq. The first layer is an x-y plot using dots to plot a
versus b. The second layer is an x-y plot using dots to plot c versus
d. The graph's coordinate system is xxx." But maps it into something
like:

gg = new (ggplot)
gg.data = qq

gg.layer[1].style = points
gg.layer[1].data = (:a, :b)

gg.layer[2].style = points
gg.layer[2].data = (:c, :d)

gg.coords = "xxx"

gg.plot ()

(where I've made up the ":a" to indicate that a is chosen from the
object's default data.) There is an obvious class hierarchy here, but
the statements are not nested, just as in ggplot2. And in fact, you
can rearrange those statements rather arbitrarily, setting gg.coords
before the layers or after the layers, etc, just as in ggplot2.

Does that make sense?

Wayne

Not at all!  It is organized in terms of the logical relationships

OK, I'll take that as a paraphrase. Note the interesting use of "the
graph's" coordinate system as opposed to "its" coordinate system.
That expresses the structure of the relationship of the coordinate
system to the graph as a whole (as opposed to one of the layers).
That is the kind of structure I am talking about.

> But maps it into something like:
>
>    gg = new (ggplot)
>    gg.data = qq

> object's default data.) There is an obvious class hierarchy here, but
> the statements are not nested, just as in ggplot2. And in fact, you
> can rearrange those statements rather arbitrarily, setting gg.coords

is good or bad, but it is definitely something you have to learn....

it easy to create graphs that elegantly tell the story of data. If

Yes, I learned R by reading Muenchen's "R for SAS and SPSS Users"
book, which is quite glowing about ggplot2. But I had no knowledge of
base graphics or anything else before starting to use ggplot. The only
command-line plotting tool I'd used recently is matlab, which is very
procedural and traditional (and limited).

JoHO says:
>I would like to second that. My impression after reading your first
>question and "rant" is that your problem comes from knowing too much
>already. Your preconceived ideas are impairing your learning of
>ggplot. To re-use your metaphor: have you ever noticed how hard it is

>in a blast?. So, even though this is just commonplace talk, I think
>you should try to forget a bit what you know and come to ggplot with a

Easier said than done! I actually study the role of prior knowledge in
conceptual learning. It's pretty hard to turn off relying on concepts
that you know when you're learning something new. People are
analogical creatures, and trying to wish it away doesn't work very
well.

Like I've said before, I really like the idea of building up a "plan"
for a graph, independent of the data, then applying the data to it.
And I really like the way ggplot fills in the blanks in your
specification in such an elegant way. But I'm not totally convinced
that the linear construction of the specification is conceptually
clearest. I realize it violates a lot of the basics of R and ggplot,
but you (read "I") almost want a GUI to put the pieces together.
Something a little like Simulink in Matlab, maybe. You wouldn't
manipulate the *data*, like in Excel, but instead you manipulate the
pieces of the data structure that define the plot. A box for a layer,
with sub-boxes for a layer's components. Shared components get linked
together (visually). Aesthetics map from the data frame to parameters
of a geom object. This tool could show what the equivalent code would
be (for educational purposes if nothing else), and could generate the
R object that you could use to make a plot. Hadley, you need an
intern!

Thanks everyone for the comments and suggestions,

-Harlan

I'm not advocating make it complicated for complexity's sake. Rather,
I am looking at ggplot2 compared to every other alternative that I'm
aware of -- especially in R -- and I love it for the difference, for
its philosophy. You seem to be arguing that it should in fact be more
like everything else, or at least the parts of "everything else" that
you've become familiar and comfortable with.

It's like you want to learn Lisp because of all the cool things it can
do, except you hate those parentheses, and you hate prefix notation,
and you'd rather have functions named similarly to C, and..., and at
some point you've created C again, perhaps with a "taste of Lisp" in
there somewhere. (Or you want to learn Spanish, but can't roll your
R's, and don't like the word ordering, and don't like the concept of
gender, and... soon you have English.)

So yes, as someone who has adopted ggplot2 because of the way it is
different from everything else, I say "it's got a long learning curve,
but it's worth it". Please don't turn ggplot2 into lattice with a
couple of fancier graph types.

> Something a little like Simulink in Matlab, maybe. You wouldn't
> manipulate the *data*, like in Excel, but instead you manipulate the
> pieces of the data structure that define the plot. A box for a layer,
> with sub-boxes for a layer's components. Shared components get linked

A nice vision, and perhaps I misunderstood you, above! At the same
time, I've seen graphical programming environments that look pretty,
but actually take a LOT more work (and are more confusing) than
something more linear. Why can't I hook up a wire from this port to
that port? Why does this box seem to work synchronously, while that is
asynchronously, and what kind of buffer do I need between them? I want
to reuse something I did, and doing a copy/paste, then going into all
of the dialog boxes to fix things is slower than tediously rewiring a
new setup. Etc...

(Not to mention that R doesn't even have useful, standardized,
interactive graphical environments yet, much less the ggplot5 you're
talking about. ;-))

On May 18, 2009, at 11:51 AM, Stavros Macrakis wrote:
> On Mon, May 18, 2009 at 9:52 AM, Wayne Folta <wd...@mac.com> wrote:
>> ...I've rewritten this reply multiple times, and finally think I

>> see the
>> core issue here: your "really means" rephrasing of the ggplot2 code
>> is
>> execution-oriented.
>

> Not at all! It is organized in terms of the logical relationships
> among the parts: where do the geoms look to find the data they refer
> to (they look in the parent ggplot)? What plots are affected by coords
> or scales (all of them)? etc.

I think the data=qq part is different from the rest of the argument to
the extent that it is a scoping-like rule that is radically different
from every language out there, including basic R. So it is confusing
in one sense, and perhaps could be eliminated from ggplot2 without
major trauma to the overall philosophy. At the same time, every
formula-using function I can think of in R has a data= which works the
same way, so it's not like Hadley made this up out of nowhere. (And in
fact, there are several advantages with doing it this way, confusing
though it may be initially.)

Leaving data= aside, I still hearing you talking in low-level,
executable terms. "Where do geoms look", "what plots are affected by",
etc, and I think that this is technically correct, but not the way to
think of ggplot2. Just as you can take "mean (a$x)" at face value, or
you can begin to get into: mean depends on a$x, which depends on a,
which is implemented as a linked list of linked lists, and mean() may
be a generic function, which depends on the class of x, and ..., and
soon you're lost in the weeds of compiler design. If you want it to
be, "mean (a$x)" is deeply hierarchical in a number of ways, both
explicit and implicit, and if you allow yourself to look at it as if
you were a C programmer implementing R it will be confusing rather
than illuminating.

A ggplot2 object contains a data frame from which it draws the data it
plots (data=). It has a coordinate system type to map from data space
to display space (coord). It has attributes describing one or more
subsets of data that should be displayed (aes, etc). Each subset of
the data (subset in terms of both columns and rows of data) can be
preprocessed mathematically, replacing or augmenting the data (stat).
Each subset can have a different presentation of the (possibly
preprocessed) points in aggregate (geom) and also individually
(scale). Etc.

Is a stat below or above a geom, or neither? Is a scale above or below
a coord, or neither? Is choosing columns of data to display (aes)
above or below choosing rows, or neither? Is a geom below a coord? You
seem to imagine that the geom "draws", looking to the coord to
determine how to draw. But it could as likely be that the geom "draws"
and its pixels are warped by the coord. Both of those are
implementation details: the meaningful distinction is that a ggplot
object displays using a coord and overlaying multiple geoms.

So, going back to the original rant, is ggplot2 hiding all kinds of
meaningful hierarchy with weird syntax? Is it making you guess things
that are implicit that should be explicit? I say no, with the arguable
exception of data=.

There's a long learning curve to ggplot2, but I think it's mostly
because of what we've used before, that has trained us to think in a
certain way about graphs, and that has trained us to expect its
functionality to fall along the grain instead of across.

I think the data=qq part is different from the rest of the argument to
the extent that it is a scoping-like rule that is radically different
from every language out there, including basic R. So it is confusing
in one sense, and perhaps could be eliminated from ggplot2 without
major trauma to the overall philosophy. At the same time, every
formula-using function I can think of in R has a data= which works the
same way, so it's not like Hadley made this up out of nowhere. (And in
fact, there are several advantages with doing it this way, confusing
though it may be initially.)

Leaving data= aside, I still hearing you talking in low-level,
executable terms. "Where do geoms look", "what plots are affected by",
etc, and I think that this is technically correct, but not the way to
think of ggplot2. Just as you can take "mean (a$x)" at face value, or
you can begin to get into: mean depends on a$x, which depends on a,
which is implemented as a linked list of linked lists, and mean() may
be a generic function, which depends on the class of x, and ..., and
soon you're lost in the weeds of compiler design. If you want it to
be, "mean (a$x)" is deeply hierarchical in a number of ways, both
explicit and implicit, and if you allow yourself to look at it as if
you were a C programmer implementing R it will be confusing rather
than illuminating.

A ggplot2 object contains a data frame from which it draws the data it
plots (data=). It has a coordinate system type to map from data space
to display space (coord). It has attributes describing one or more
subsets of data that should be displayed (aes, etc). Each subset of
the data (subset in terms of both columns and rows of data) can be
preprocessed mathematically, replacing or augmenting the data (stat).
Each subset can have a different presentation of the (possibly
preprocessed) points in aggregate (geom) and also individually
(scale). Etc.

Is a stat below or above a geom, or neither? Is a scale above or below
a coord, or neither? Is choosing columns of data to display (aes)
above or below choosing rows, or neither? Is a geom below a coord? You
seem to imagine that the geom "draws", looking to the coord to
determine how to draw. But it could as likely be that the geom "draws"
and its pixels are warped by the coord. Both of those are
implementation details: the meaningful distinction is that a ggplot
object displays using a coord and overlaying multiple geoms.

So, going back to the original rant, is ggplot2 hiding all kinds of
meaningful hierarchy with weird syntax? Is it making you guess things
that are implicit that should be explicit? I say no, with the arguable
exception of data=.

There's a long learning curve to ggplot2, but I think it's mostly
because of what we've used before, that has trained us to think in a
certain way about graphs, and that has trained us to expect its
functionality to fall along the grain instead of across.
